Hexamita in Aquarium Fish: Diagnosis and Treatment

facts.fact: The flagellates once called Hexamita sp. in angelfish are diplomonads.
Diplomonads were found in about 50% of angelfish examined at the University of Florida fish disease laboratory.
Their clinical importance is debated because they are often found in fish that look healthy.
Spironucleus is an internal flagellate that lives in the lower intestine.
Spironucleus affects all cichlids, bettas, gouramis and many other aquarium fish.
Hexamita is a flagellated protozoan of the intestinal tract. Discus, oscars and angelfish are especially vulnerable to it.
Many fish carry low numbers of Hexamita without showing signs.
Spironucleus signs include weight loss (anorexia) and deaths of fry and juveniles.
Diagnosis is made with a wet mount.
Infection is graded by counting organisms per low-power field in an intestinal exam: slight 1-5, moderate 5-15, marked 15-30, extreme 30-100.
Angelfish with heavy lab infections often showed no other abnormalities.
Signs include appetite loss with white, mucus-trailing feces, darkened colour, hiding and hovering near the surface.
Small pits can form around the sensory pores of the head and grow into craters if not treated.
Treat at once if a fish refuses food for more than three days while passing stringy feces.
Early signs in discus are going off food, white stringy mucous feces and rapid weight loss.
Later signs are a swollen belly, dull skin, lethargy and hiding in corners.
Severe cases lie near the bottom, with a swollen red anus and possible belly ulcers.
White stool in discus can also come from stress, diet (spinach, Spirulina, peas, Epsom salt, unsoaked dry food), worms or internal bacterial infection, not only Hexamita.
A keeper described a sick fish as dark and lethargic with cotton-like white stringy feces and a sunken head and belly.
After shipping, diplomonad counts in angelfish rose sharply within 24 hours, to more than 500 organisms per low-power field.
Infections not controlled before shipping may cause deaths within one week.
Overcrowding, poor water quality or a poor diet can make Hexamita multiply quickly.
Vitamin C and D deficiency has been linked to Hexamita susceptibility in cichlids.
Causes of gut disease in discus include spoiled food, overfeeding, high NH3/NO2, Hexamita/Spironucleus, and stress from sudden temperature changes or overcrowding.
Hexamita is called the most notorious cause of white stool in discus. Parasites can enter with new plants, fish or objects.
A beef-heart-only diet, too much fiber or fat, and sudden diet changes can cause digestive upset in discus.
Isolate the sick fish in a separate tank kept at 28-30°C with strong aeration.
Treat in a bare-bottom quarantine tank of at least 40 litres instead of the display tank.
Medicate every fish in the tank, because infected fish can reinfect the others.
Metronidazole is listed as the treatment for Spironucleus, for non-food fish only.
Before shipping, angelfish were treated with metronidazole in feed at 50 mg/kg for 5 days.
Another group was treated with a metronidazole bath at 5 mg/L for 3 hours daily for 5 days.
Treated fish had 0-1 organisms per field after shipping, against more than 500 in controls, and none of the treated fish died.
Metronidazole bath: 250 mg per 40 litres every 48 hours for three treatments, with a 25% water change before each dose.
Medicated food: soak food in 500 mg metronidazole dissolved in 30 ml of tank water and feed only this for 7–10 days. Food is preferred while fish still eat.
Remove activated carbon during treatment because it adsorbs the drug.
Metronidazole is toxic to shrimp and snails.
Tank dose: 1 gram metronidazole per 20 gallons, given for 10 days straight.
For fish not eating, raise the tank to 86 to 88 (Fahrenheit implied) during treatment.
Metronidazole stays active in water for about eight hours, so a water change can follow eight hours after dosing.
Medicated food made in advance loses effect. Feed it right away and coat lightly, because too much makes the food bitter and fish refuse it.
Metronidazole is said not to harm the biological filter, and UV is reported safe to keep running.
Vietnamese method: 1 tablet of Metronidazol per 20 litres as a 2-day soak, then siphon about half the water, refill and redose for the new water, at 32–33°C.
Alternative: an oral digestive enzyme product (e.g. BIO FISH) per label, with the temperature raised to 32–33°C.
Do not feed during treatment and resume about 3 days after it ends. Mosquito larvae are suggested as easy-to-digest food.
A forum keeper gives metronidazole at 500 mg per 40 litres, dissolved in warm water, in a hospital tank with strong aeration.
A keeper suggests a bath of about 5 mg/L every other day for three treatments, or food at about 50 mg/kg body weight (10 mg per gram food) for five days, citing UF/IFAS.
A keeper reports raising the temperature to 96°F for five days worked with discus. They said it was untested in angelfish.
Test ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, pH and oxygen first and fix water quality with regular water changes.
Preventive metronidazole before shipping may reduce sickness after shipping.
Keep ammonia and nitrite at zero and nitrate below 20 ppm, avoid overstocking, and feed varied quality food instead of mostly dry flake.
Quarantine new fish for at least two weeks. Discus keepers often give a preventive medicated food course during quarantine.
Medicated food for two or three feedings every three months is suggested as prevention.
Change 20–30% of the water weekly, keep pH 6.5–7.0, and remove uneaten food after each feeding.
Quarantine new fish for 2 weeks and use probiotics or digestive supplements.
Avoid high-risk live feeder fish, or rinse or quarantine them before feeding.
Do not combine several medicines without instructions or raise the dose on your own.
Dosing one tablet a day in a bucket is criticised. The dose should follow water volume and the drug's directions.
Overdosing metronidazole is warned against because it can kill fish.
Treating in the display tank can upset the biological filter.
In Vietnam the disease is often called 'phân trắng' or 'bệnh đường ruột' in discus (cá đĩa/cá dĩa), and metronidazol tablets are the common treatment.
Vietnamese keepers recommend raising the temperature to 32–33°C during treatment.
Vietnamese forum keepers disagree on feeding during illness: one says fast the fish, another says feed bloodworms (trùn huyết).
A Vietnamese forum keeper says raising the temperature generally does not help this disease, against common advice.
A moderator says metronidazole alone may not stick well and mixed it into food, or used a product like API General Cure.
